summaryEn: A Taiwanese contract manufacturer that bought its way into becoming a global fitness brand — Matrix in gyms, Horizon and BowFlex at home, Fujiiryoki in massage chairs. Gross margin above 50% proves the brand strategy worked; the extreme seasonality and a US$40m tariff refund landing as one-off income both need reading carefully.
model: editorial (truth-audited: FinMind + company earnings call; OEM-to-brand framing — 51% gross margin, the 71/22/7 commercial-home-massage mix, 44 subsidiaries across 38 countries and the BowFlex/Fujiiryoki acquisitions credited, but the extreme Q4-vs-Q1 seasonality flagged against annualising any quarter, the weak 2026Q1 attributed to the company's own stated expense causes rather than a margin problem, and the US$30m tariff refund identified in advance as non-operating other income; sector Biotech & Healthcare → Fitness Equipment)

sections.bodyMarkdown:
Johnson Health Tech (喬山健康科技, TWSE: 1736) makes exercise equipment and massage chairs — and, unusually for a Taiwanese manufacturer, it **sells them under its own brands**. Founded in **October 1975** and **listed in January 2003**, it began as a contract manufacturer and spent five decades converting itself into a branded consumer business: **MATRIX** and **ONYX** in commercial gyms, **VISION** in the mid-market, **Horizon**, **BowFlex**, **Schwinn** and **JRNY** at home, and **Fujiiryoki** and **SYNCA** in massage chairs. It operates **44 marketing subsidiaries across 38 countries** and **300 owned retail outlets**.

The proof that the brand strategy worked is in the gross margin. Johnson runs at **around 51%** — a level no contract manufacturer achieves, and one that puts it closer to a consumer brand than to the ODMs elsewhere in this collection. The 2025 revenue mix was **commercial 71%, home 22%, massage chairs 7%**, with **North America at 45% of revenue** and Latin America at 7% and growing. Earnings recovered sharply: annual EPS ran **NT$1.42 (FY2022) → 2.33 → 8.01 (FY2024) → NT$9.07 (FY2025)**, with FY2024 profit up roughly **242%**. Trailing return on equity is **17.7%**, and the dividend rose from **NT$1.0 (FY2023) to NT$4.0 (FY2024) and NT$4.5 (FY2025)** — a **3.45% yield** at NT$130.50, on **15.9× earnings**.

Two things about the numbers demand care. First, **the seasonality is extreme**: 2025Q4 EPS was **NT$5.65** against **NT$0.08 in 2026Q1**, and December revenue of **NT$8.80bn** against January's **NT$3.86bn**. Annualising any single quarter of this company produces nonsense in either direction. Second, and more subtly, Johnson expects a **US$40m US tariff refund**, of which **US$30m will be booked as "other income" in 2026Q2–Q3** — a **non-operating one-off that will flatter reported profit** — with the remaining US$10m reducing cost of goods sold.

The weak 2026Q1 is worth stating precisely: the **operating margin was −0.78%**, but **gross margin recovered to 51.3%** from 48.6%. By the company's own account the problem was **expenses** — roughly NT$100m+ of 50th-anniversary costs and a deferred US$2m charge — not pricing or product. The honest read: **a genuine brand-building success with real 50% margins and a credible tariff-mitigation plan — reporting through a seasonally distorted, one-off-laden year that requires reading the operating line, not the headline.**

Johnson Health Tech was founded in **1975** in Taichung, making exercise equipment for other companies to sell. That was the standard Taiwanese model: build to someone else's specification, compete on cost and reliability, and accept the thin margin that comes with anonymity. For a fitness-equipment maker it meant supplying treadmills and strength machines to Western brands that owned the customer relationship — and captured most of the value.

The company's defining decision was to stop doing that. Over decades it built and bought its way into **owning brands**, which meant taking on everything an OEM avoids: product design, dealer networks, advertising, service, retail. It **listed in 2003**, and built a distribution footprint of **44 marketing subsidiaries in 38 countries** and **300 owned retail outlets** — infrastructure that only makes sense if you own the brand at the end of it.

The portfolio was assembled deliberately, across price points and categories. **MATRIX** and **ONYX** address commercial gyms at the premium end, **VISION** the mid-market. At home, **Horizon** was joined in 2024 by **BowFlex**, **Schwinn** and the **JRNY** digital platform — bought out of a **bankruptcy auction, approved by the court on 15 April 2024 and closed a week later, for roughly US$37.5m (about NT$1.2bn)**. Distressed pricing for brands with decades of US consumer recognition. In massage chairs, Johnson acquired **Fujiiryoki** of Japan outright, adding a category adjacent to fitness with its own installed base.

The result is visible in a single number: a company that began as a contract manufacturer now runs a **gross margin around 51%**. FY2024 profit rose roughly **242%** as the acquisitions took effect. The strategy was not to make equipment more cheaply than anyone else — it was to stop selling it to someone who would put their own name on it.

- **1975 (7 Oct)** — Johnson Health Tech founded in Taichung as a contract manufacturer of exercise equipment.
- **1980s–1990s** — Shifts from pure OEM toward owning brands and building overseas distribution.
- **2003 (9 Jan)** — **Lists on the Taiwan Stock Exchange (1736)**.
- **2000s–2010s** — Builds out **MATRIX** (premium commercial), **VISION** (mid-market) and **Horizon** (home); expands to **44 marketing subsidiaries in 38 countries** with **300 owned retail outlets**.
- **Fujiiryoki acquisition** — Buys 100% of Japan's Fujiiryoki, adding massage chairs; the group has internally discussed listing it separately in Japan.
- **2024 (April)** — **Acquires BowFlex, Schwinn and JRNY out of a US bankruptcy auction** for roughly **US$37.5m (~NT$1.2bn)**; court approval 15 April, closing 22 April.
- **2024** — Acquisitions land: **FY2024 EPS NT$8.01**, profit up roughly **242%**; Q4 alone earns **NT$5.94**. Dividend lifted from NT$1.0 to **NT$4.0**.
- **2025** — **FY2025 EPS NT$9.07**; dividend **NT$4.5**. Gross margin dips to **48.6%** in Q4 on US tariffs; Vietnam reaches **30% of capacity**.
- **2026Q1** — Gross margin recovers to **51.3%**, but operating margin is **−0.78%** on 50th-anniversary costs (~NT$100m+) and a deferred US$2m charge; **EPS NT$0.08**.
- **2026 (May)** — Guides commercial growth ~20% and home growth above 20%; discloses a **US$40m tariff refund** (US$30m as other income in Q2–Q3, US$10m against COGS), with **US$2.8m already received**; **Vietnam plant 2 to reach full production in Q3**.

Johnson's accounts show **an acquisition-driven brand business with excellent margins and a deeply seasonal shape**.

- **A sharp, acquisition-led recovery.** Annual EPS: **NT$1.42 (FY2022) → 2.33 (FY2023) → 8.01 (FY2024) → NT$9.07 (FY2025)**, with **FY2024 profit up roughly 242%** as the BowFlex and Fujiiryoki acquisitions took effect. Trailing **return on equity is 17.7%**.
- **The margin is the evidence.** **Gross margin around 51%** — 52.7% at its 2025Q1 peak, 48.6% at the tariff-driven 2025Q4 trough, back to **51.3% in 2026Q1**. A contract manufacturer does not earn this; a brand does.
- **Seasonality that invalidates single-quarter analysis.** **2025Q4 EPS NT$5.65 against 2026Q1's NT$0.08.** December revenue **NT$8.80bn** versus January's **NT$3.86bn**. Roughly two-thirds of a year's profit lands in the fourth quarter. **Annualising any quarter of this company is meaningless.**
- **2026Q1 was an expense problem, not a margin problem.** Operating margin **−0.78%** and net margin **0.20%**, but **gross margin rose to 51.3%**. The company attributes the higher expense ratio to roughly **NT$100m+ of 50th-anniversary costs** and a **deferred US$2m charge**, and guides an ongoing expense ratio of **43–45%**.
- **A one-off that will flatter coming quarters.** Of the **US$40m US tariff refund**, **US$30m relates to goods already sold and will be recognised as "other income" in 2026Q2–Q3** — **non-operating**, and not a sign of improving trade. The other **US$10m** reduces cost of goods sold on unsold inventory, genuinely lifting future gross margin. **US$2.8m had been received as of May 2026.**
- **A dividend that stepped up with earnings.** Cash dividends (FinMind, by fiscal year): **NT$1.4 (2019) → 1.12 → 0.5 → 0.6 → 1.0 (2023) → 4.0 (2024) → NT$4.5 (2025)** — a **3.45% yield** at NT$130.50.
- **Leverage and valuation.** **NT$46.4bn of assets** on **NT$14.1bn of equity**, a **69.6% debt ratio**, **NT$3.16bn of cash**; **15.9× earnings and 2.81× book**.

The financing reality: **a successful brand roll-up earning consumer-grade margins**, carrying meaningful leverage, and reporting through a year in which **one-offs and seasonality both distort the headline in the same direction**.

**Stance: a Taiwanese OEM that genuinely became a global consumer brand — 51% gross margins, 17.7% ROE, 15.9x earnings — reporting through a seasonally distorted year with a large non-operating one-off ahead.**

The bull case:

1. **The brand transformation is complete and measurable.** **Gross margin around 51%** is not achievable as a contract manufacturer. Johnson owns **MATRIX, ONYX, VISION, Horizon, BowFlex, Schwinn, JRNY, Fujiiryoki and SYNCA**, sold through **44 subsidiaries in 38 countries** and **300 owned stores**.
2. **Acquisitions have been bought well and integrated.** **BowFlex, Schwinn and JRNY** were acquired out of bankruptcy for roughly **US$37.5m** — decades of US consumer recognition at distressed prices — and **FY2024 profit rose about 242%**.
3. **A credible tariff answer, not just a complaint.** Production is being split by destination: **China plants serve non-US markets, Taiwan and Vietnam serve the US.** **Vietnam plant 2 reaches full production in 2026Q3**, and capacity is being built toward supporting **NT$100bn of annual revenue**. Guidance is for **~20% commercial and >20% home growth** with gross margin rising about a point a quarter.
4. **Reasonably priced.** **15.9× earnings, 2.81× book, 3.45% yield** with **ROE 17.7%**.

The counter-arguments:

- **Coming quarters will be flattered by a one-off.** **US$30m of the tariff refund lands as non-operating "other income" in Q2–Q3.** Reported profit will rise for a reason that will not repeat.
- **Seasonality invites misreading in both directions.** **Q4 EPS NT$5.65 versus Q1's NT$0.08.** Neither is representative.
- **Consumer discretionary demand is cyclical**, and home fitness in particular whipsawed severely through the pandemic and after.
- **Leverage.** A **69.6% debt ratio** on **NT$14.1bn of equity**, after an acquisition-led expansion.
- **Tariff exposure is unresolved, only mitigated.** North America is **45% of revenue**; the refund is compensation for a cost that was real.

An **owner-of-brands** thesis: buy the margin structure and the distribution, and read the **operating line** rather than the headline for the next two quarters.

Johnson makes money by **owning the brand at the point of sale**, across three segments and two channels:

- **Commercial (71% of 2025 revenue).** Equipment for gyms, hotels, corporate facilities and clubs, under **MATRIX** (premium), **ONYX** (luxury) and **VISION** (mid-market). Institutional buyers purchase on durability, service and total cost of ownership rather than price alone, and replacement cycles are long — which makes this the more stable, higher-margin half of the business.
- **Home (22%).** **Horizon**, plus **BowFlex**, **Schwinn** and the **JRNY** digital training platform acquired in 2024. Consumer demand here is far more cyclical and far more seasonal — the fourth quarter and the new-year resolution season carry a disproportionate share of the year.
- **Massage chairs (7%).** **Fujiiryoki** and **SYNCA**, an adjacent premium durable with its own retail dynamic.
- **The distribution asset.** **44 marketing subsidiaries in 38 countries** and **300 owned retail outlets**. This is expensive infrastructure — it is also the reason Johnson captures a **51% gross margin** instead of an OEM's teens, and it is not something a competitor replicates quickly.
- **Manufacturing arranged around tariffs.** **China plants serve non-US markets; Taiwan and Vietnam serve the United States.** Vietnam was **30% of capacity in 2025**, with a second plant reaching full production in **2026Q3** and capacity being built toward supporting **NT$100bn of annual revenue**.

The economics are **brand economics with a manufacturing base**: a high gross margin funding a **43–45% operating expense ratio**, leaving an operating margin that swings with seasonality and one-off costs. **North America is 45% of revenue.**

The strength is that Johnson owns both ends — it manufactures and it sells under its own name, so it captures the full spread. The vulnerability is symmetrical: it also carries **both** an OEM's fixed manufacturing costs **and** a brand's fixed selling costs, so a soft quarter compresses profit from both sides. That is precisely what 2026Q1 showed — **51.3% gross margin, −0.78% operating margin**.

Fitness equipment is two industries wearing one label, and Johnson is unusual in competing in both.

- **Commercial equipment is an institutional business.** Gyms, hotels and clubs buy on **durability, serviceability and total cost of ownership**, with long replacement cycles and relationships that persist across them. Margins are better and demand is steadier. The competitive set is global: **Life Fitness, Technogym, Precor** and Johnson's **MATRIX**.
- **Home equipment is a consumer business with brutal cycles.** The pandemic pulled years of demand forward, then reversed it — **Peloton** and **Nautilus (BowFlex's former parent)** are the well-known casualties. Johnson's response was to **buy the wreckage**: BowFlex, Schwinn and JRNY out of bankruptcy for roughly **US$37.5m**, acquiring brand recognition that would cost far more to build.
- **Massage chairs are a premium durable adjacent to fitness**, with a strong Japanese heritage — which is what the **Fujiiryoki** acquisition bought.
- **Why manufacturing location has become strategic.** US tariffs directly hit anyone shipping fitness equipment from China into a market that is **45% of Johnson's revenue**. The industry response has been to relocate, and Johnson's split — **China for non-US markets, Taiwan and Vietnam for the US** — is the concrete version of that. Its **US$40m refund** is the accounting aftermath of the cost already incurred.
- **What separates Johnson from Taiwanese peers.** Most Taiwanese manufacturers in this collection sell to brands. Johnson **is** the brand, which is why its gross margin is **51%** rather than the single digits of a server ODM like Wiwynn. The trade-off is that it also carries the brand's cost base.

Johnson's position is **strongest in commercial equipment**, where institutional relationships and service networks compound, and **most exposed in home**, where consumer sentiment turns quickly. The industry truth is that **owning a brand converts a manufacturing margin into a consumer margin — and a manufacturing cyclicality into a consumer one.**

**Strengths**
- **Owned-brand portfolio across price points**: MATRIX, ONYX, VISION (commercial), Horizon, BowFlex, Schwinn, JRNY (home), Fujiiryoki, SYNCA (massage).
- **~51% gross margin** and **17.7% trailing ROE** — consumer-brand economics from a former OEM.
- **44 subsidiaries in 38 countries, 300 owned retail outlets**; commercial is **71% of revenue**, the steadier half.
- **Acquisitions bought cheaply**: BowFlex/Schwinn/JRNY out of bankruptcy for roughly **US$37.5m**; FY2024 profit up ~242%.

**Weaknesses**
- **Extreme seasonality**: 2025Q4 EPS **NT$5.65** versus 2026Q1's **NT$0.08**; December revenue **NT$8.80bn** versus January's **NT$3.86bn**.
- **2026Q1 operating margin −0.78%** on 50th-anniversary and deferred costs; expense ratio guided at **43–45%**.
- **69.6% debt ratio** after acquisition-led expansion; **NT$3.16bn of cash** against **NT$46.4bn of assets**.

**Opportunities**
- **Vietnam plant 2 at full production in 2026Q3**; capacity being built toward supporting **NT$100bn of revenue**.
- Guidance of **~20% commercial and >20% home growth**, with gross margin rising about a point a quarter.
- **US$10m of the tariff refund** genuinely reducing COGS on unsold inventory; Latin America (7%) growing fast.

**Threats**
- **Consumer discretionary cyclicality**, especially in home fitness after the post-pandemic reversal.
- **Further tariff action** against a business with **45% of revenue in North America**.
- **US$30m of the refund is non-operating other income** — reported profit in Q2–Q3 will not be repeatable.

- **Coming results will be distorted by a one-off, in the flattering direction.** **US$30m of the US$40m tariff refund will be recognised as "other income" in 2026Q2–Q3** — **non-operating**, and non-recurring. Reported net profit will jump for a reason that has nothing to do with the business improving. The correct comparison is the **operating line**.
- **Seasonality makes single quarters actively misleading.** **2025Q4 EPS was NT$5.65; 2026Q1 was NT$0.08.** Extrapolating either produces a wildly wrong picture. Only full-year or trailing-twelve-month figures are meaningful for this company.
- **Consumer discretionary exposure.** Home fitness (22% of revenue) is among the most cyclical consumer categories, as the post-pandemic collapse of Peloton and Nautilus demonstrated — the latter being the very business Johnson bought out of bankruptcy.
- **Tariff exposure is mitigated, not removed.** **North America is 45% of revenue.** The Vietnam and Taiwan capacity split addresses current tariffs; further trade action would require further response, and the refund is compensation for a cost already paid.
- **Leverage after an acquisition-led expansion.** A **69.6% debt ratio** on **NT$14.1bn of equity**, with **NT$3.16bn of cash**. Integration of BowFlex, Schwinn, JRNY and Fujiiryoki carries execution risk alongside the debt.
- **Cost control.** The company guides an expense ratio of **43–45%**; 2026Q1 exceeded it enough to push the operating margin negative despite a **51.3% gross margin**. With a high fixed-cost brand infrastructure, expense discipline is the difference between a good quarter and a loss.

Johnson's outlook depends on whether **brand economics and the new manufacturing footprint deliver the guided growth once the one-offs wash out.** The axes to watch:

- **Operating margin — the line that matters.** 2026Q1 was **−0.78%** despite a **51.3% gross margin**. Because **US$30m of the tariff refund lands in "other income"**, net profit for Q2–Q3 will look strong regardless; the operating margin is where genuine improvement will or will not appear.
- **Gross margin trajectory.** Guidance is roughly **+1 point per quarter**, with a bigger step once **Vietnam plant 2 reaches full production in Q3**, and a stated ambition to exceed the **52.7% peak**. The **US$10m COGS credit** on unsold inventory helps here — legitimately.
- **Segment growth against guidance.** **~20% commercial** and **>20% home** (helped by BowFlex sales resuming with advertising support). Commercial is the steadier 71%; home is where the guidance carries more risk.
- **Full-year, not quarterly, earnings.** With **Q4 carrying the bulk of profit**, the FY2026 outcome will not be visible until the year is nearly over. FY2025's **NT$9.07** is the benchmark.

Bottom line: Johnson Health Tech is the rare Taiwanese manufacturer that **successfully stopped being one** — **51% gross margins**, a nine-brand portfolio across commercial, home and massage, **44 subsidiaries in 38 countries**, and **17.7% ROE** at **15.9× earnings** with a **3.45% yield**. The qualifiers are that its **fourth quarter carries the year** (Q4 EPS NT$5.65 versus Q1's NT$0.08), that **US$30m of incoming tariff refund is non-operating income** which will flatter the next two quarters, and that it carries a **69.6% debt ratio** into a cyclical consumer market. Judge it on **full-year operating profit** — a real brand, reported through a noisy year.
